title: Methods
intro: Methods go in an `impl` block. The first parameter says how the method uses the struct: read it, change it, or take it.

coming_from.go: An `impl` block holds the methods, and `&mut self` is your pointer receiver. A Go value receiver gets a copy; in Rust, plain `self` takes the value itself, and the caller can't use it again unless the type is `Copy`. `&self` is a pointer receiver that can only read, which Go can't say. `Counter::new()` is a naming habit, like `NewCounter()`.
coming_from.kotlin: Methods go in a separate `impl` block, and there is no constructor: `new` is an ordinary function, like a factory in a companion object. A method that changes the struct takes `&mut self`, and a variable that owns the struct must be `let mut` to call it, where Kotlin lets a `val` call anything.
coming_from.python: `self` is written out like Python's, but its form says what the method does: `&self` reads, `&mut self` changes, plain `self` uses it up. There is no `__init__`: `Counter::new()` is just a function that returns a `Counter`.
coming_from.typescript: `this` becomes an explicit `self` parameter, and its form says what the method does: `&self` reads, `&mut self` changes. There is no `class` or `new`: `Counter::new()` is a plain function, and a variable that owns the object must be `let mut` to call a `&mut self` method.
coming_from.java: Methods live in a separate `impl` block, and `this` is written out as the first parameter, with a mode: `&self` reads, `&mut self` changes, `self` takes the value. There are no constructors, so `Counter::new()` is a plain function, and two methods of one type can't share a name. A variable that owns the object must be `let mut` to call a `&mut self` method.
coming_from.csharp: An `impl` block holds the methods, and `fn new()` with no `self` is a `static` factory, since Rust has no constructors. The receiver says whether a method changes the struct (`&mut self`) or only reads it (`&self`), which C# classes never spell out.
coming_from.c: This is your `counter_bump(struct Counter *c)` pattern with the call written `c.bump()`: `&self` is like `const struct Counter *` and `&mut self` like `struct Counter *`. Where gcc only warns about passing a `const` object to a non-`const` pointer, Rust refuses to build.
coming_from.cpp: `&self` is a `const` member function and `&mut self` is a non-`const` one, but the default flips: values are immutable unless declared `let mut`. There are no constructors; `Counter::new()` is an ordinary associated function that returns a value.

notes: `&self` lets the method read the struct without copying it. `&mut self` lets the method change it. `self` (no &) means the method takes the struct; after calling it the caller can't use it (unless the type is `Copy`), and the method may hand it back.
`new` is not a keyword. It is just the usual name for a constructor function.
You call methods with a dot either way. Rust adds the `&` or `&mut` for you.

Two methods written in a type's own `impl` blocks can't share a name, so you can't overload by parameter list. Constructors get different names instead: `new`, `with_capacity`, `from_parts`. ([Traits](/learn/traits/), covered later, can give one name several meanings, as `From` does for `from`.)

gotcha.title: Calling a changing method on a non-mut variable
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, `c.Bump()` works on any variable: Go takes `&c` for you. In Kotlin, `val c` only stops reassigning `c`; the object inside can still change.
gotcha.rust_sees: `bump` says "I change the counter" (`&mut self`). But `c` was declared with plain `let`, which means "this never changes".
gotcha.why: In Rust, `let` without `mut` covers the whole value, including everything inside it. That is stronger than Java's `final`, Kotlin's `val` or a JavaScript `const`, which only stop the variable from pointing somewhere else. It is what lets you trust that a non-mut value really stays the same (a few types, such as `Cell` and `Mutex`, change through `&` on purpose; see Shared state).

go.says: Go runs this and prints 1. Go takes `&c` for you behind the scenes when `c` is a variable, so it can call a pointer method.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints 1. `val` only stops you from reassigning `c`, not from changing what's inside it.

python.says: Python prints 1. There is no `mut`: any name can call any method, and the object changes. An ordinary class has no way to mark a method as "changes the object" or a variable as "never changes" (a frozen dataclass opts in per class).

typescript.says: Prints 1. `const` only stops you from pointing `c` at a different object; the object itself can still change. (`readonly` fields opt in, one by one.)

java.says: This prints 1. In Java, `final` only stops `c` from pointing at another object; the object itself can still change.

csharp.says: A method can change a class's (non-`readonly`) fields in C#, so this prints 1. There is no marker at the call site that says this call changes `c`.

c.says: gcc only warns that `&c` drops the `const`, then lets `counter_bump` change it and prints 1. Changing a const object is undefined behaviour, so this is luck.

python.code:
class Counter:
    def __init__(self) -> None:  # called as Counter()
        self.count = 0

    def get(self) -> int:
        return self.count

    def bump(self) -> None:  # any method can change self
        self.count += 1


c = Counter()
c.bump()
c.bump()
print(c.get())
